chapter: Race, unions and the color line
title: Was Yellow Nunez white? Sidney Arodin and Lazy River
summary: Argument over whether Yellow Nunez and Sidney Arodin were part Black, with Lala insisting the family said Nunez was white; a remark on Lazy River's original title.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: No, I thought he was yellow.
No. No, I didn't know he was white. He didn't know how colored he was. No, I heard that, though. No, I'll tell you.

You'd be surprised the guys I heard was colored. The reason why we called him yellow, because he was a colored guy. I heard Steven Allen had colored in it. Huh? I heard Steven Allen had colored in it. Oh, I didn't know about Steven Allen. The reason why we called him yellow. He was yellow.

You see? That's a bad thing to say. That's why we called him yellow. Because he was olive complexion, you see? That's a bad thing to say. That's why we called him yellow. Because he was olive complexion, you see? Sam Charles told me about yellow. He knew that. No, he wasn't one of those. Papa Lane and Mama Lane said that he was white. He was white. Yeah. They knew it. The parents and the whole family. Now, he's white. Was that about Steven Allen?
I don't believe it. I heard that from Thomas Berry. I heard that from Thomas Berry. I said something about Doc Suchon. No, yellow wasn't. The other thing's going.

I don't believe it about Sidney Allen. Is he living in Sidney? No, but I'm the white as Sidney Allen. Well, I understand when he first wrote Lazy Ripper, he called it Lazy Lazy Nigger. That was the first thing we heard of him, huh?
